title: 1.5.17 A1.5.2 — Computational Thinking
description: Explain the four parts of computational thinking in your own words, with a worked example of each. AI-graded with hints.

aiGrader.prompt:
Explain computational thinking in your own words.

Part 1 — The four parts. For each one below, write 1-2 sentences saying what it means:
1. Decomposition - breaking a big problem into smaller pieces you can handle one at a time
2. Pattern recognition - noticing where those pieces repeat, or resemble something you have solved before
3. Abstraction - ignoring the details that do not matter for the problem you are solving
4. Algorithmic thinking - putting the pieces into a precise sequence of steps someone else could follow

Part 2 — One example each. Give one concrete example of each of the four, drawn from one program you have actually written this quarter - a lab from module 1.2 or 1.3. If you truly cannot find all four in one program, an everyday task is accepted instead, but try the code first. Name the task, then say what the decomposition, the pattern, the abstraction and the algorithm were in that specific case.

Use your own words. Do not copy definitions from the internet.

rubric.title: All four parts explained
rubric.description: Student addresses all four of decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking in Part 1, each by name (or an unmistakable synonym) and each with at least one sentence of explanation. Credit requires all four. Covering three does not earn this criterion.

rubric.title: Explanations are in the student's own words
rubric.description: The definitions read as a beginner's own understanding rather than copied text. Look for personal phrasing and natural variation. Deny if the wording matches dictionary or textbook definitions verbatim.

rubric.title: A specific task is named in Part 2
rubric.description: Student names one concrete thing they actually did - preferably a specific program or lab they wrote this quarter ('the ten broken declarations lab', 'my object description'), or failing that a specific everyday activity. Generic references such as 'a problem', 'some code' or 'an assignment' do not count.

rubric.title: All four parts are illustrated with that task
rubric.description: Student gives an example of each of the four parts, and the examples are drawn from the task they named rather than being restatements of the definitions. Deny if an example just repeats the definition in different words, or if fewer than four are illustrated.

rubric.title: The abstraction example names something deliberately ignored
rubric.description: Abstraction is the part beginners most often get wrong by describing simplification in general. Credit requires the student to name at least one specific detail they left out and why it did not matter for this problem - for example 'it does not matter what brand of bread it is'. Deny if the abstraction example does not identify something omitted.
